title: Constrained Edit Fields for Training-Free Flow Editing

paper.title: Constrained Edit Fields for Training-Free Flow Editing
paper.abstract: Abstract Text-guided image editing aims to perform a desired edit while preserving source content unrelated to it. Pretrained rectified-flow models enable training-free editing of real images through modifications to their sampling trajectories. However, responses at locations unrelated to the desired edit can still accumulate along the editing trajectory and become visible in the final result. To overcome this, we propose Constrained Edit Fields (CEF) , which assigns each spatial location a continuous edit responsibility that quantifies its relevance to the desired edit. CEF estimates edit responsibility directly from the source image when the relevant content is present. For edits whose target content is absent from the source, CEF first generates an unconstrained proposal to reveal its realized spatial support and then estimates responsibility from that proposal. At each editing step, CEF decomposes the base edit field into prompt-induced and trajectory-induced components, enabling edit responsibility to preserve instruction-relevant updates while suppressing unintended trajectory-induced changes. Evaluated on all 700 PIE-Bench examples, CEF achieves state-of-the-art Structure Distance, background LPIPS, and background MSE with both Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium and FLUX, while retaining competitive instruction alignment. On Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium, it reduces these metrics over the previous best results by 10.2%, 21.2%, and 48.0%, respectively.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Text-guided image editing aims to modify a source image according to an editing instruction while preserving content unrelated to the desired edit. Rectified-flow models ( Lipman et al. 2023 ; Liu, Gong, and Liu 2023 ) such as SD3 and FLUX have demonstrated strong text-to-image generation capabilities ( Esser et al. 2024 ; Stability AI 2024 ; Black Forest Labs 2024 ) . Training-free editing methods leverage these pretrained models to edit real images by modifying their sampling trajectories, without task-specific finetuning ( Xu et al. 2025 ; Avrahami et al. 2025 ; Wang et al. 2025 ; Kim et al. 2025 ; Kulikov et al. 2025 ; Xie et al. 2025 ; Yang and Ye 2026 ) . In flow-based editing, the source and target descriptions yield different velocity predictions at each sampling step, and their difference forms the edit field that updates the editing trajectory ( Kulikov et al. 2025 ) . However, this field spans the entire latent grid and can introduce updates at locations unrelated to the desired edit. As shown in Figure 1 , the editor closes the subject’s eyes as instructed and substantially alters his appearance and facial structure. Figure 1: Effect of constraining the edit field. The unconstrained edit field introduces updates across the latent grid, closing the subject’s eyes while substantially altering his appearance. CEF constrains these updates according to edit responsibility, completing the desired edit while preserving the source appearance. Existing training-free methods improve source preservation by refining editing trajectories ( Mokady et al. 2023 ; Xu et al. 2025 ; Wang et al. 2025 ; Xie et al. 2025 ; Yang and Ye 2026 ) , reusing source representations ( Hertz et al. 2023 ; Tumanyan et al. 2023 ; Cao et al. 2023 ; Avrahami et al. 2025 ; Kim et al. 2025 ; Yang et al. 2026 ) , or providing spatial guidance ( Avrahami, Lischinski, and Fried 2022 ; Couairon et al. 2023 ; Zhu et al. 2025 ; Long et al. 2026 ; Jiao et al. 2026 ; Cui et al. 2026 ) . However, the cumulative effect of spatially diffuse edit responses along the trajectory remains insufficiently characterized. Although such responses may be weak at individual steps, repeated integration can amplify them into visible source degradation. As shown in Figure 2 , the cumulative field displacement outside the edited region reaches 27.0% of the total unconstrained update within the edited region, and visualizations of the image differences show unrelated facial changes progressively emerging during sampling. These observations demonstrate that weak stepwise responses can accumulate into substantial deviations, highlighting the need to account for each location’s relevance to the desired edit. Figure 2: Accumulation of unintended changes. (a) Cumulative field displacement outside the edited region, relative to the total unconstrained update inside it. CEF suppresses it while preserving most edited-region updates. (b) Pixel differences along the unconstrained trajectory reveal the intended edit and progressively emerging facial changes. We propose Constrained Edit Fields (CEF) , which assigns each spatial location a continuous edit responsibility that quantifies how much of its local update is admitted into the constrained edit field. CEF estimates this responsibility from the CLIPSeg responses that localize the content involved in the desired edit ( Lüddecke and Ecker 2022 ) . The editing instruction identifies the relevant content, and visual evidence reveals its realized spatial support. For content observable in the source image, CEF computes responsibility directly from the source response. For content absent from the source, CEF first uses an unconstrained base editor to generate a proposal and estimates responsibility from its response to reveal the realized spatial support. CEF then reuses the sampled noise sequence used to generate the proposal during the constrained edit. The proposal and constrained edit therefore share the sampled noise sequence while following different latent trajectories. At each editing step, the base edit field compares a target-prompt velocity on the editing trajectory with a source-prompt velocity on the source trajectory, and therefore combines changes in both the prompt and trajectory. CEF exactly decomposes this field into prompt-induced and trajectory-induced changes. The prompt-induced change provides a directional reference for distinguishing the aligned component of the trajectory-induced change. Edit responsibility then modulates their spatial contributions, imposing stronger constraints on the remaining trajectory-induced change where responsibility is low. The resulting constrained field updates the editing trajectory. Experiments on all 700 PIE-Bench examples ( Ju et al. 2024 ) using Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium ( Esser et al. 2024 ; Stability AI 2024 ) and FLUX ( Black Forest Labs 2024 ) demonstrate that CEF consistently improves source preservation while maintaining strong editing instruction alignment. CEF establishes new best results for Structure Distance, background LPIPS, and background MSE on both backbones. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We show that weak responses at locations unrelated to the desired edit accumulate along the sampling trajectory, and propose edit responsibility to spatially regulate the edit field according to each location’s relevance. • We propose CEF, which estimates edit responsibility from visual evidence in the source image or an unconstrained proposal, and exactly decomposes the base edit field into prompt-induced and trajectory-induced changes. • Experiments on all 700 PIE-Bench examples using Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium and FLUX demonstrate that CEF achieves state-of-the-art source preservation while faithfully aligning with the editing instructions.

sections.heading: Training-Based Editing.
sections.text: Training-based approaches learn instruction-conditioned image transformations from editing data. InstructPix2Pix trains a diffusion model on synthetic editing examples to follow natural-language editing instructions ( Brooks, Holynski, and Efros 2023 ) . Emu Edit broadens the range of supported editing operations through multi-task training ( Sheynin et al. 2024 ) , and OmniEdit trains a generalist editor under the supervision of multiple specialist models ( Wei et al. 2025 ) . More recently, FLUX.1 Kontext unifies image generation and editing within a flow-matching framework jointly conditioned on a source image and text ( Black Forest Labs et al. 2025 ) . Their editing capabilities require editing-specific data and model training. Figure 3: Overview of Constrained Edit Fields. Source or proposal evidence localizes the content involved in the edit and yields a continuous edit responsibility. At each step, the base edit field is exactly decomposed into prompt-induced and trajectory-induced changes. CEF uses the prompt-induced direction to form prompt-aligned and residual trajectory components, applying responsibility more strongly to the residual to construct the constrained edit field.

sections.heading: Training-Free Editing.
sections.text: Training-free editing directly leverages pretrained generative models by constructing or modifying their inference trajectories. Early diffusion-based approaches obtain editable representations of the source by altering the sampling initialization or improving the inversion process. SDEdit performs target-conditioned sampling from a partially noised source image ( Meng et al. 2022 ) , and Null-text Inversion optimizes unconditional text embeddings to improve real-image inversion and reconstruction ( Mokady et al. 2023 ) . For rectified-flow models, FTEdit, RF-Inversion, RF-Edit, and FireFlow improve inversion through fixed-point refinement, stochastic inversion, and specialized numerical solvers ( Xu et al. 2025 ; Rout et al. 2025 ; Wang et al. 2025 ; Deng et al. 2025 ) . Another family of methods improves source preservation through representation reuse or trajectory alignment. Stable Flow selectively injects attention features from structure-preserving layers ( Avrahami et al. 2025 ) ; ReFlex extracts intermediate source features and adapts attention during editing ( Kim et al. 2025 ) ; DNAEdit aligns the underlying noise ( Xie et al. 2025 ) ; and DirectEdit establishes step-level alignment between reconstruction and inversion paths ( Yang and Ye 2026 ) . Recent inversion-free methods construct editing trajectories without explicit inversion. FlowEdit combines source- and target-conditioned velocity fields ( Kulikov et al. 2025 ) ; SplitFlow composes prompt-specific sub-flows ( Yoon et al. 2025 ) ; FIA-Edit introduces frequency-interactive attention ( Yang et al. 2026 ) ; FlowAlign regularizes the editing trajectory ( Kim et al. 2026 ) ; and ChordEdit constructs a temporally averaged low-energy control field for one-step editing ( Lu et al. 2026 ) . These advances improve reconstruction accuracy, trajectory consistency, and source preservation. But, the spatial extent of the resulting updates remains a separate concern.

sections.heading: Spatially Constrained Editing.
sections.text: Spatially constrained methods determine which image regions are affected by an edit. Blended Diffusion incorporates a user-provided mask into the denoising process ( Avrahami, Lischinski, and Fried 2022 ) , and DiffEdit estimates semantic edit regions by contrasting predictions conditioned on the source and target prompts ( Couairon et al. 2023 ) . KV-Edit preserves background key–value tokens outside user-specified regions ( Zhu et al. 2025 ) , and ReFlex uses attention-derived regions for latent blending ( Kim et al. 2025 ) . Recent approaches further derive spatial cues from the generation process. Follow-Your-Shape constructs a Trajectory Divergence Map from token-wise velocity differences between inversion and editing trajectories to control key–value injection ( Long et al. 2026 ) . UniEdit-Flow constructs edit regions from per-step velocity differences ( Jiao et al. 2026 ) . DirectEdit uses MLLM localization and Segment Anything masks for noise blending, together with attention feature injection ( Kirillov et al. 2023 ; Yang and Ye 2026 ) . SAM-Flow combines responses from the source and a scout image to construct dynamic editing support and perform source-anchored projection ( Cui et al. 2026 ) . Across these methods, spatial signals determine where editing updates are applied, with source preservation enforced through blending, feature injection, or trajectory correction. CEF represents visual relevance as continuous edit responsibility and uses it within the base edit field to regulate prompt-induced and trajectory-induced changes.

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: Given a source image x src x_{\mathrm{src}} and source and target prompts c src c_{\mathrm{src}} and c tar c_{\mathrm{tar}} , let z t src z_{t}^{\mathrm{src}} and z t edit z_{t}^{\mathrm{edit}} denote the source and editing trajectories. At each editing step, the difference between the velocity predicted on the editing trajectory under the target prompt and that predicted on the source trajectory under the source prompt forms the base edit field. CEF associates each spatial location with a continuous edit responsibility estimated from visual evidence. CEF then exactly decomposes the base edit field into prompt-induced and trajectory-induced changes at each step, and uses edit responsibility to regulate their contributions to the constrained edit field. sections.heading: Edit Responsibility from Visual Evidence
sections.text: Preserving source content unrelated to the desired edit requires identifying the image locations involved in the edit. The editing instruction specifies the desired semantic change, and visual evidence localizes the corresponding content in the image. CEF represents each location’s relevance to the desired edit as continuous edit responsibility. This responsibility determines the contribution of the local update to the constrained edit field. Locations with larger responsibility retain more of the edit-induced update. Locations with smaller responsibility are more strongly constrained. The evidence used to estimate responsibility depends on whether the relevant content is observable in the source image. Observable content can be localized directly from the source, which provides source evidence. Content absent from the source provides no corresponding visual evidence. In this case, CEF first generates an unconstrained proposal x ~ \widetilde{x} in which the target content has been realized and uses it as visual evidence for estimating responsibility. Given an evidence image x x and a query q q describing the content involved in the desired edit, CLIPSeg ( Lüddecke and Ecker 2022 ) g ϕ g_{\phi} produces a spatial response. CEF converts this response into the edit responsibility r = ℛ ⁡ ( g ϕ ​ ( x , q ) ) , r=\mathcal{R}\!\left(g_{\phi}(x,q)\right), (1) where ℛ \mathcal{R} converts the CLIPSeg response into a continuous responsibility field at the spatial resolution of the edit field. We use x = x src x=x_{\mathrm{src}} for source evidence and x = x ~ x=\widetilde{x} for proposal evidence. CEF estimates r r once from the selected evidence and keeps it fixed throughout the editing trajectory. For proposal evidence, let Ω \Omega denote the sampled noise sequence used to generate x ~ Ω \widetilde{x}_{\Omega} , from which CEF estimates r Ω r_{\Omega} . Since a different sequence may place the target content elsewhere, CEF reuses Ω \Omega during the constrained edit. The proposal and constrained edit therefore share the sampled noise sequence while following different latent trajectories.

sections.heading: Decomposing the Edit Field
sections.text: Let v t ​ ( z , c ) v_{t}(z,c) denote the guided velocity predicted at step t t for latent z z under prompt c c . The base edit field compares predictions that differ in two respects: the target velocity is evaluated on the editing trajectory under the target prompt, whereas the source velocity is evaluated on the source trajectory under the source prompt. Following the differential formulation of training-free flow editing ( Kulikov et al. 2025 ) , the base edit field is A t = v t ​ ( z t edit , c tar ) − v t ​ ( z t src , c src ) . A_{t}=v_{t}\!\left(z_{t}^{\mathrm{edit}},c_{\mathrm{tar}}\right)-v_{t}\!\left(z_{t}^{\mathrm{src}},c_{\mathrm{src}}\right). (2) The field therefore combines the effect of changing the prompt with the effect of moving from the source trajectory to the editing trajectory. Therefore, treating it as a single quantity does not distinguish the contributions arising from these two sources. To solve this, CEF proposes to separate the two effects without changing the base edit field. The four relevant velocity predictions pair the source and editing states with the source and target prompts. Holding the latent state fixed while changing the prompt isolates a prompt-induced velocity change. For a fixed state z z , we write Δ t prompt ​ ( z ) = v t ​ ( z , c tar ) − v t ​ ( z , c src ) . \Delta_{t}^{\mathrm{prompt}}(z)=v_{t}(z,c_{\mathrm{tar}})-v_{t}(z,c_{\mathrm{src}}). (3) The prompt-induced velocity change depends on the state at which it is evaluated. CEF evaluates it on both trajectories and averages the results to obtain the prompt-induced change, P t = 1 2 ​ [ Δ t prompt ​ ( z t src ) + Δ t prompt ​ ( z t edit ) ] . P_{t}=\frac{1}{2}\left[\Delta_{t}^{\mathrm{prompt}}(z_{t}^{\mathrm{src}})+\Delta_{t}^{\mathrm{prompt}}(z_{t}^{\mathrm{edit}})\right]. (4) Conversely, holding the prompt fixed while moving from the source state to the editing state isolates a trajectory-induced velocity change, Δ t traj ​ ( c ) = v t ​ ( z t edit , c ) − v t ​ ( z t src , c ) . \Delta_{t}^{\mathrm{traj}}(c)=v_{t}(z_{t}^{\mathrm{edit}},c)-v_{t}(z_{t}^{\mathrm{src}},c). (5) This change depends on the prompt under which the two states are compared. CEF evaluates it under both prompts and averages the results to obtain the trajectory-induced change, S t = 1 2 ​ [ Δ t traj ​ ( c src ) + Δ t traj ​ ( c tar ) ] . S_{t}=\frac{1}{2}\left[\Delta_{t}^{\mathrm{traj}}(c_{\mathrm{src}})+\Delta_{t}^{\mathrm{traj}}(c_{\mathrm{tar}})\right]. (6) By construction, the two terms form an exact additive decomposition of the base edit field, A t = P t + S t . A_{t}=P_{t}+S_{t}. (7) Consequently, the decomposition preserves the update prescribed by the base editor while explicitly seperating the prompt-induced and trajectory-induced changes. sections.heading: The Constrained Edit Field
sections.text: Decomposing the base field allows CEF to distinguish the part of the trajectory-induced change that follows the prompt-induced direction. The positive projection S t + S_{t}^{+} follows the local direction of P t P_{t} . We refer to P t + S t + P_{t}+S_{t}^{+} as the prompt-aligned component and to S t − S t + S_{t}-S_{t}^{+} as the residual trajectory component . CEF uses edit responsibility to regulate these two components differently. It applies r r to the prompt-aligned component P t + S t + P_{t}+S_{t}^{+} and r 2 r^{2} to the residual trajectory component. The constrained edit field can be formulated as A ~ t = r ⊙ ( P t + S t + ) + r 2 ⊙ ( S t − S t + ) , \widetilde{A}_{t}=r\odot\left(P_{t}+S_{t}^{+}\right)+r^{2}\odot\left(S_{t}-S_{t}^{+}\right), (9) where ⊙ \odot denotes the Hadamard product, with r r and r 2 r^{2} broadcast across the channel dimension. At any location with r > 0 r>0 , the ratio between the coefficients applied to the residual trajectory component and the prompt-aligned component is r r . As edit responsibility decreases, the residual trajectory component is therefore attenuated more rapidly, changing both the magnitude and composition of the local update rather than uniformly scaling the base edit field. The construction preserves the two endpoints of edit responsibility. At a location with r = 1 r=1 , the two terms recombine as P t + S t = A t P_{t}+S_{t}=A_{t} ; at a location with r = 0 r=0 , the constrained update vanishes. sections.heading: Evaluation Datasets and Metrics.
sections.text: We evaluate CEF on all 700 examples in PIE-Bench ( Ju et al. 2024 ) . We measure alignment with the target prompt using CLIP similarity ( Radford et al. 2021 ) between the prompt and either the complete edited image (CLIP-W) or the annotated edit region (CLIP-E). Source preservation is evaluated using DINO-based Structure Distance ( Ju et al. 2024 ; Caron et al. 2021 ) over the complete image, together with PSNR, MSE, LPIPS ( Zhang et al. 2018 ) , and SSIM ( Wang et al. 2004 ) over the region outside the edit. Benchmark masks define the edited region and the remaining image only for evaluation and are not accessed by CEF.

sections.heading: Implementation Details.
sections.text: We implement CEF using Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium ( Esser et al. 2024 ; Stability AI 2024 ) and FLUX ( Black Forest Labs 2024 ) as the backbone models, while keeping all generative models frozen. For direct comparison, we use the sampling configurations of FlowEdit ( Kulikov et al. 2025 ) : ( T , n max ) = ( 50 , 33 ) (T,n_{\max})=(50,33) for SD3.5 and ( T , n max ) = ( 28 , 24 ) (T,n_{\max})=(28,24) for FLUX, with n avg = 1 n_{\mathrm{avg}}=1 for both. The classifier-free guidance scales ( Ho and Salimans 2022 ) for the source and target are 3.5 3.5 and 13.5 13.5 for SD3.5, and 1.5 1.5 and 5.5 5.5 for FLUX. The source prompt, target prompt, and editing instruction determine the evidence used by CEF and the content queried by CLIPSeg. For multiple grounding phrases, CEF takes a pixel-wise maximum over their CLIPSeg responses, bilinearly resizes the combined response to image resolution, and applies per-image min–max normalization to obtain s ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] s\in[0,1] , in this order. CEF then maps s s to image-space responsibility using clip ⁡ ( α ​ s γ , 0 , 1 ) \operatorname{clip}(\alpha s^{\gamma},0,1) , where α \alpha is the responsibility gain and γ \gamma is the response exponent. The resulting responsibility map is resized to the spatial resolution of the edit field. SD3.5 uses ( α , γ ) = ( 2.3 , 1.5 ) (\alpha,\gamma)=(2.3,1.5) for source evidence and ( 1.0 , 1.0 ) (1.0,1.0) for proposal evidence; FLUX uses ( 4.0 , 1.0 ) (4.0,1.0) for both. For global edits, we set r ≡ 1 r\equiv 1 over the spatial grid, so A ~ t = A t \widetilde{A}_{t}=A_{t} and CEF reduces to the base editor. Benchmark categories and masks are not used. Experiments are conducted in a Linux container on NVIDIA A800-SXM4 GPUs with 80 GB of memory, using Python 3.11 and PyTorch 2.11 with CUDA 12.8. Responsibility construction and processing details are provided in Appendix A . Runtime and memory analyses are provided in Appendix B .

sections.heading: Comparison Methods.
sections.text: For quantitative comparison, we use the published PIE-Bench aggregates reported by DirectEdit ( Yang and Ye 2026 ) . They cover diffusion-based editors InstructPix2Pix ( Brooks, Holynski, and Efros 2023 ) and Prompt-to-Prompt ( Hertz et al. 2023 ) , together with the rectified-flow methods FTEdit ( Xu et al. 2025 ) , RF-Inversion ( Rout et al. 2025 ) , RFEdit ( Wang et al. 2025 ) , FireFlow ( Deng et al. 2025 ) , FlowEdit ( Kulikov et al. 2025 ) , FlowAlign ( Kim et al. 2026 ) , and DNAEdit ( Xie et al. 2025 ) . DirectEdit and its mask-free variant are taken from the same report. We run SAM-Flow ( Cui et al. 2026 ) on all 700 examples using the authors’ implementation and evaluate it with the same protocol.

sections.heading: Main Results
sections.text: Table 1 reports results on all 700 PIE-Bench examples. CEF achieves the best Structure Distance and all four metrics measured outside the edited region on SD3.5. Compared with DNAEdit, the previous best Structure Distance result, CEF reduces it from 11.03 to 9.91. Compared with DirectEdit, the previous strongest baseline on the background metrics, CEF reduces LPIPS from 31.36 to 24.72 and MSE from 21.64 to 11.26, while attaining a higher CLIP-E. FlowEdit obtains the highest CLIP scores but performs substantially worse on the preservation metrics. Figure 4 compares CLIP-E and background PSNR for three values of n max n_{\max} . Across these settings, CEF achieves higher PSNR than FlowEdit at similar CLIP-E. The main CEF configuration also has higher PSNR than all SD3.5 baselines in the table. Complete frontier metrics are provided in Appendix D . On FLUX, CEF also achieves the best Structure Distance, background LPIPS, MSE, and SSIM while retaining competitive CLIP-E, confirming consistent preservation gains across both backbones.

sections.heading: Qualitative comparison.
sections.text: Figure 5 compares four local edits across the two backbones. FlowEdit often completes the requested edit but may also change nearby content or the appearance of the source object, as shown by the cake and bird examples. FlowAlign and DNAEdit sometimes leave the requested edit incomplete or change the pose and scale of the edited object. DirectEdit and SAM-Flow localize the edit more accurately but can still alter the source appearance or introduce local artifacts. Across both backbones, CEF changes the cake geometry while retaining its frosting and surroundings, opens the panda’s mouth without altering its facial appearance, transforms the dog while preserving its pose and background, and adds the bird without changing the apple or table. Additional qualitative results are provided in Appendix E ; failure cases and limitations are discussed in Appendix F .

sections.heading: Decomposition improves preservation.
sections.text: To isolate the effect of decomposition, we apply a single fixed coefficient to S t S_{t} across all locations and active editing steps. Since A t = P t + S t A_{t}=P_{t}+S_{t} , a coefficient of 1 1 on S t S_{t} exactly recovers the original FlowEdit field. We set the coefficient to 0.5 0.5 as a simple non-adaptive control; this coefficient is not selected as an optimum. The resulting field P t + 0.5 ​ S t P_{t}+0.5S_{t} retains all 24 active steps. We then shorten FlowEdit to 20 active steps to match its editing strength. The two settings produce nearly identical CLIP-E values of 20.90 and 20.91. As shown in Figure 9 , the decomposed field reduces Structure Distance from 8.99 to 6.54, LPIPS from 53.02 to 43.41, and MSE from 29.07 to 22.68. Separately attenuating S t S_{t} therefore provides better source preservation than reducing the number of active FlowEdit steps with nearly identical CLIP-E.

sections.heading: Effect of replay.
sections.text: We evaluate replay on all 80 PIE-Bench edits that add an object. For the controlled comparison, both final constrained edits use the same fixed realization Ω \Omega . With replay, responsibility r Ω r_{\Omega} is estimated from the proposal generated with Ω \Omega ; without replay, responsibility r Ω ′ r_{\Omega^{\prime}} is estimated from an independently generated proposal with Ω ′ \Omega^{\prime} . This isolates the effect of realization-matched proposal evidence. Figure 7 shows that replay makes the final edit more closely retain the location and extent of the added content in the proposal. Across all 80 edits, the overlap between the added-object regions in the proposal and final result increases from 0.708 to 0.794. The paired 95% bootstrap confidence interval indicates an increase of 4.6 to 12.8 percentage points.

sections.heading: Hyperparameter sensitivity.
sections.text: Table 9 varies α \alpha and γ \gamma one at a time around the values used in the main FLUX experiments. Across the evaluated values, CLIP-E changes by only 0.14, while Structure Distance and LPIPS change gradually. Larger values of γ \gamma reduce both preservation errors while CLIP-E remains similar. The main setting, ( α , γ ) = ( 4.0 , 1.0 ) (\alpha,\gamma)=(4.0,1.0) , was not selected using this subset and is not best in any reported metric. Complete sensitivity results are provided in Appendix C .

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: We propose CEF, a training-free method, to address unintended source changes caused by edit responses accumulating outside the requested region along editing trajectories. CEF estimates continuous edit responsibility from visual evidence, decomposes the base edit field into prompt-induced and trajectory-induced components, and spatially constrains their contributions at each editing step. This design suppresses unrelated changes without uniformly weakening the editing trajectory. Across all 700 PIE-Bench examples, CEF achieves state-of-the-art source preservation with SD3.5 Medium and FLUX while maintaining edit alignment.

sections.heading: Visual evidence selection.
sections.text: CEF derives grounding phrases and selects the visual evidence source from the source description, target description, and editing instruction. When the edit-related content is observable in the source image, CEF estimates edit responsibility from the source image. When the requested target content is generated by the edit, CEF first runs the base editor to produce a proposal and estimates responsibility from the realized target content. For global edits, CEF sets r ≡ 1 r\equiv 1 . The evidence source and grounding phrases are determined before constrained generation begins.

sections.heading: Responsibility construction.
sections.text: For each grounding phrase, the frozen CLIPSeg model ( Lüddecke and Ecker 2022 ) produces an image-space semantic response. CEF combines responses from multiple phrases by a pixel-wise maximum, bilinearly resizes the combined response to image resolution, and applies per-image min–max normalization to obtain s ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] s\in[0,1] . It maps the semantic response to edit responsibility as r = clip ⁡ ( α ​ s γ , 0 , 1 ) . r=\operatorname{clip}(\alpha s^{\gamma},0,1). (11) CEF then resizes the responsibility to the spatial resolution of the latent edit field using area interpolation. The responsibility is computed once and held fixed over all active editing steps. SD3.5 ( Esser et al. 2024 ; Stability AI 2024 ) uses ( α , γ ) = ( 2.3 , 1.5 ) (\alpha,\gamma)=(2.3,1.5) for source evidence and ( 1.0 , 1.0 ) (1.0,1.0) for proposal evidence. FLUX ( Black Forest Labs 2024 ) uses ( 4.0 , 1.0 ) (4.0,1.0) for both evidence sources.

sections.heading: Proposal evidence and stochastic replay.
sections.text: For edits using proposal evidence, CEF first runs the base editor to produce an unconstrained proposal and evaluates the target grounding phrase on the realized proposal. During constrained editing, CEF replays the noise sequence sampled for proposal generation. The proposal and constrained edit share the same noise realization and evolve along their respective latent trajectories. The resulting responsibility corresponds to the target content realized under that noise sequence.

sections.heading: Sampling configurations.
sections.text: SD3.5 uses 50 sampling steps, n max = 33 n_{\max}=33 , n avg = 1 n_{\mathrm{avg}}=1 , and source and target guidance scales of 3.5 and 13.5. FLUX uses 28 sampling steps, n max = 24 n_{\max}=24 , n avg = 1 n_{\mathrm{avg}}=1 , and source and target guidance scales of 1.5 and 5.5. sections.heading: Appendix F Failure Cases and Limitations
sections.text: Figure A2 shows two representative failures with their post-hoc field diagnostics. In the example involving a spatial relation, the grounding phrase cups places responsibility on the surrounding cups rather than the central clock hands identified by the benchmark edit region. Although the raw field contains a response around the clock hands, the constrained field attenuates it; the hands remain near their source pose while the cups are altered. This illustrates that noun-grounded responsibility can miss the visual carrier of a relational change. In the deletion example, responsibility overlaps the cat and the constrained field is localized to that region. The cat is removed, but the vacated region is completed with painting tools instead of a clean continuation of the scene. This is a scene-completion ambiguity rather than a localization failure: spatial responsibility determines where the model may edit, but it does not uniquely determine content that was occluded by the removed object. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2609.33735v1 [cs.CV] 27 Sep 2026 Constrained Edit Fields for Training-Free Flow Editing Jingxuan Kang Yinsong Wang Che Liu Chen Qin \corresponding Abstract Text-guided image editing aims to perform a desired edit while preserving source content unrelated to it. Pretrained rectified-flow models enable training-free editing of real images through modifications to their sampling trajectories. However, responses at locations unrelated to the desired edit can still accumulate along the editing trajectory and become visible in the final result. To overcome this, we propose Constrained Edit Fields (CEF) , which assigns each spatial location a continuous edit responsibility that quantifies its relevance to the desired edit. CEF estimates edit responsibility directly from the source image when the relevant content is present. For edits whose target content is absent from the source, CEF first generates an unconstrained proposal to reveal its realized spatial support and then estimates responsibility from that proposal. At each editing step, CEF decomposes the base edit field into prompt-induced and trajectory-induced components, enabling edit responsibility to preserve instruction-relevant updates while suppressing unintended trajectory-induced changes. Evaluated on all 700 PIE-Bench examples, CEF achieves state-of-the-art Structure Distance, background LPIPS, and background MSE with both Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium and FLUX, while retaining competitive instruction alignment. On Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium, it reduces these metrics over the previous best results by 10.2%, 21.2%, and 48.0%, respectively. Imperial College London j.kang26@imperial.ac.uk, c.qin15@imperial.ac.uk Introduction Text-guided image editing aims to modify a source image according to an editing instruction while preserving content unrelated to the desired edit. Rectified-flow models ( Lipman et al. 2023 ; Liu, Gong, and Liu 2023 ) such as SD3 and FLUX have demonstrated strong text-to-image generation capabilities ( Esser et al. 2024 ; Stability AI 2024 ; Black Forest Labs 2024 ) . Training-free editing methods leverage these pretrained models to edit real images by modifying their sampling trajectories, without task-specific finetuning ( Xu et al. 2025 ; Avrahami et al. 2025 ; Wang et al. 2025 ; Kim et al. 2025 ; Kulikov et al. 2025 ; Xie et al. 2025 ; Yang and Ye 2026 ) . In flow-based editing, the source and target descriptions yield different velocity predictions at each sampling step, and their difference forms the edit field that updates the editing trajectory ( Kulikov et al. 2025 ) . However, this field spans the entire latent grid and can introduce updates at locations unrelated to the desired edit. As shown in Figure 1 , the editor closes the subject’s eyes as instructed and substantially alters his appearance and facial structure. Figure 1: Effect of constraining the edit field. The unconstrained edit field introduces updates across the latent grid, closing the subject’s eyes while substantially altering his appearance. CEF constrains these updates according to edit responsibility, completing the desired edit while preserving the source appearance. Existing training-free methods improve source preservation by refining editing trajectories ( Mokady et al. 2023 ; Xu et al. 2025 ; Wang et al. 2025 ; Xie et al. 2025 ; Yang and Ye 2026 ) , reusing source representations ( Hertz et al. 2023 ; Tumanyan et al. 2023 ; Cao et al. 2023 ; Avrahami et al. 2025 ; Kim et al. 2025 ; Yang et al. 2026 ) , or providing spatial guidance ( Avrahami, Lischinski, and Fried 2022 ; Couairon et al. 2023 ; Zhu et al. 2025 ; Long et al. 2026 ; Jiao et al. 2026 ; Cui et al. 2026 ) . However, the cumulative effect of spatially diffuse edit responses along the trajectory remains insufficiently characterized. Although such responses may be weak at individual steps, repeated integration can amplify them into visible source degradation. As shown in Figure 2 , the cumulative field displacement outside the edited region reaches 27.0% of the total unconstrained update within the edited region, and visualizations of the image differences show unrelated facial changes progressively emerging during sampling. These observations demonstrate that weak stepwise responses can accumulate into substantial deviations, highlighting the need to account for each location’s relevance to the desired edit. Figure 2: Accumulation of unintended changes. (a) Cumulative field displacement outside the edited region, relative to the total unconstrained update inside it. CEF suppresses it while preserving most edited-region updates. (b) Pixel differences along the unconstrained trajectory reveal the intended edit and progressively emerging facial changes. We propose Constrained Edit Fields (CEF) , which assigns each spatial location a continuous edit responsibility that quantifies how much of its local update is admitted into the constrained edit field. CEF estimates this responsibility from the CLIPSeg responses that localize the content involved in the desired edit ( Lüddecke and Ecker 2022 ) . The editing instruction identifies the relevant content, and visual evidence reveals its realized spatial support. For content observable in the source image, CEF computes responsibility directly from the source response. For content absent from the source, CEF first uses an unconstrained base editor to generate a proposal and estimates responsibility from its response to reveal the realized spatial support. CEF then reuses the sampled noise sequence used to generate the proposal during the constrained edit. The proposal and constrained edit therefore share the sampled noise sequence while following different latent trajectories. At each editing step, the base edit field compares a target-prompt velocity on the editing trajectory with a source-prompt velocity on the source trajectory, and therefore combines changes in both the prompt and trajectory. CEF exactly decomposes this field into prompt-induced and trajectory-induced changes. The prompt-induced change provides a directional reference for distinguishing the aligned component of the trajectory-induced change. Edit responsibility then modulates their spatial contributions, imposing stronger constraints on the remaining trajectory-induced change where responsibility is low. The resulting constrained field updates the editing trajectory. Experiments on all 700 PIE-Bench examples ( Ju et al. 2024 ) using Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium ( Esser et al. 2024 ; Stability AI 2024 ) and FLUX ( Black Forest Labs 2024 ) demonstrate that CEF consistently improves source preservation while maintaining strong editing instruction alignment. CEF establishes new best results for Structure Distance, background LPIPS, and background MSE on both backbones. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We show that weak responses at locations unrelated to the desired edit accumulate along the sampling trajectory, and propose edit responsibility to spatially regulate the edit field according to each location’s relevance. • We propose CEF, which estimates edit responsibility from visual evidence in the source image or an unconstrained proposal, and exactly decomposes the base edit field into prompt-induced and trajectory-induced changes. • Experiments on all 700 PIE-Bench examples using Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium and FLUX demonstrate that CEF achieves state-of-the-art source preservation while faithfully aligning with the editing instructions. Related Work Training-Based Editing. Training-based approaches learn instruction-conditioned image transformations from editing data. InstructPix2Pix trains a diffusion model on synthetic editing examples to follow natural-language editing instructions ( Brooks, Holynski, and Efros 2023 ) . Emu Edit broadens the range of supported editing operations through multi-task training ( Sheynin et al. 2024 ) , and OmniEdit trains a generalist editor under the supervision of multiple specialist models ( Wei et al. 2025 ) . More recently, FLUX.1 Kontext unifies image generation and editing within a flow-matching framework jointly conditioned on a source image and text ( Black Forest Labs et al. 2025 ) . Their editing capabilities require editing-specific data and model training. Figure 3: Overview of Constrained Edit Fields. Source or proposal evidence localizes the content involved in the edit and yields a continuous edit responsibility. At each step, the base edit field is exactly decomposed into prompt-induced and trajectory-induced changes. CEF uses the prompt-induced direction to form prompt-aligned and residual trajectory components, applying responsibility more strongly to the residual to construct the constrained edit field. Training-Free Editing. Training-free editing directly leverages pretrained generative models by constructing or modifying their inference trajectories. Early diffusion-based approaches obtain editable representations of the source by altering the sampling initialization or improving the inversion process. SDEdit performs target-conditioned sampling from a partially noised source image ( Meng et al. 2022 ) , and Null-text Inversion optimizes unconditional text embeddings to improve real-image inversion and reconstruction ( Mokady et al. 2023 ) . For rectified-flow models, FTEdit, RF-Inversion, RF-Edit, and FireFlow improve inversion through fixed-point refinement, stochastic inversion, and specialized numerical solvers ( Xu et al. 2025 ; Rout et al. 2025 ; Wang et al. 2025 ; Deng et al. 2025 ) . Another family of methods improves source preservation through representation reuse or trajectory alignment. Stable Flow selectively injects attention features from structure-preserving layers ( Avrahami et al. 2025 ) ; ReFlex extracts intermediate source features and adapts attention during editing ( Kim et al. 2025 ) ; DNAEdit aligns the underlying noise ( Xie et al. 2025 ) ; and DirectEdit establishes step-level alignment between reconstruction and inversion paths ( Yang and Ye 2026 ) . Recent inversion-free methods construct editing trajectories without explicit inversion. FlowEdit combines source- and target-conditioned velocity fields ( Kulikov et al. 2025 ) ; SplitFlow composes prompt-specific sub-flows ( Yoon et al. 2025 ) ; FIA-Edit introduces frequency-interactive attention ( Yang et al. 2026 ) ; FlowAlign regularizes the editing trajectory ( Kim et al. 2026 ) ; and ChordEdit constructs a temporally averaged low-energy control field for one-step editing ( Lu et al. 2026 ) . These advances improve reconstruction accuracy, trajectory consistency, and source preservation. But, the spatial extent of the resulting updates remains a separate concern. Spatially Constrained Editing. Spatially constrained methods determine which image regions are affected by an edit. Blended Diffusion incorporates a user-provided mask into the denoising process ( Avrahami, Lischinski, and Fried 2022 ) , and DiffEdit estimates semantic edit regions by contrasting predictions conditioned on the source and target prompts ( Couairon et al. 2023 ) . KV-Edit preserves background key–value tokens outside user-specified regions ( Zhu et al. 2025 ) , and ReFlex uses attention-derived regions for latent blending ( Kim et al. 2025 ) . Recent approaches further derive spatial cues from the generation process. Follow-Your-Shape constructs a Trajectory Divergence Map from token-wise velocity differences between inversion and editing trajectories to control key–value injection ( Long et al. 2026 ) . UniEdit-Flow constructs edit regions from per-step velocity differences ( Jiao et al. 2026 ) . DirectEdit uses MLLM localization and Segment Anything masks for noise blending, together with attention feature injection ( Kirillov et al. 2023 ; Yang and Ye 2026 ) . SAM-Flow combines responses from the source and a scout image to construct dynamic editing support and perform source-anchored projection ( Cui et al. 2026 ) . Across these methods, spatial signals determine where editing updates are applied, with source preservation enforced through blending, feature injection, or trajectory correction. CEF represents visual relevance as continuous edit responsibility and uses it within the base edit field to regulate prompt-induced and trajectory-induced changes. Edit Responsibility from Visual Evidence Preserving source content unrelated to the desired edit requires identifying the image locations involved in the edit. The editing instruction specifies the desired semantic change, and visual evidence localizes the corresponding content in the image. CEF represents each location’s relevance to the desired edit as continuous edit responsibility. This responsibility determines the contribution of the local update to the constrained edit field. Locations with larger responsibility retain more of the edit-induced update. Locations with smaller responsibility are more strongly constrained. The evidence used to estimate responsibility depends on whether the relevant content is observable in the source image. Observable content can be localized directly from the source, which provides source evidence. Content absent from the source provides no corresponding visual evidence. In this case, CEF first generates an unconstrained proposal x ~ \widetilde{x} in which the target content has been realized and uses it as visual evidence for estimating responsibility. Given an evidence image x x and a query q q describing the content involved in the desired edit, CLIPSeg ( Lüddecke and Ecker 2022 ) g ϕ g_{\phi} produces a spatial response. We use x = x src x=x_{\mathrm{src}} for source evidence and x = x ~ x=\widetilde{x} for proposal evidence. CEF estimates r r once from the selected evidence and keeps it fixed throughout the editing trajectory. Decomposing the Edit Field Let v t ​ ( z , c ) v_{t}(z,c) denote the guided velocity predicted at step t t for latent z z under prompt c c . The base edit field compares predictions that differ in two respects: the target velocity is evaluated on the editing trajectory under the target prompt, whereas the source velocity is evaluated on the source trajectory under the source prompt. Following the differential formulation of training-free flow editing ( Kulikov et al. 2025 ) , the base edit field is A t = v t ​ ( z t edit , c tar ) − v t ​ ( z t src , c src ) . A_{t}=v_{t}\!\left(z_{t}^{\mathrm{edit}},c_{\mathrm{tar}}\right)-v_{t}\!\left(z_{t}^{\mathrm{src}},c_{\mathrm{src}}\right). (2) The field therefore combines the effect of changing the prompt with the effect of moving from the source trajectory to the editing trajectory. Therefore, treating it as a single quantity does not distinguish the contributions arising from these two sources. To solve this, CEF proposes to separate the two effects without changing the base edit field. The four relevant velocity predictions pair the source and editing states with the source and target prompts. Holding the latent state fixed while changing the prompt isolates a prompt-induced velocity change. For a fixed state z z , we write Δ t prompt ​ ( z ) = v t ​ ( z , c tar ) − v t ​ ( z , c src ) . \Delta_{t}^{\mathrm{prompt}}(z)=v_{t}(z,c_{\mathrm{tar}})-v_{t}(z,c_{\mathrm{src}}). (3) The prompt-induced velocity change depends on the state at which it is evaluated. CEF evaluates it on both trajectories and averages the results to obtain the prompt-induced change, P t = 1 2 ​ [ Δ t prompt ​ ( z t src ) + Δ t prompt ​ ( z t edit ) ] . P_{t}=\frac{1}{2}\left[\Delta_{t}^{\mathrm{prompt}}(z_{t}^{\mathrm{src}})+\Delta_{t}^{\mathrm{prompt}}(z_{t}^{\mathrm{edit}})\right]. (4) Conversely, holding the prompt fixed while moving from the source state to the editing state isolates a trajectory-induced velocity change, Δ t traj ​ ( c ) = v t ​ ( z t edit , c ) − v t ​ ( z t src , c ) . \Delta_{t}^{\mathrm{traj}}(c)=v_{t}(z_{t}^{\mathrm{edit}},c)-v_{t}(z_{t}^{\mathrm{src}},c). (5) This change depends on the prompt under which the two states are compared. CEF evaluates it under both prompts and averages the results to obtain the trajectory-induced change, S t = 1 2 ​ [ Δ t traj ​ ( c src ) + Δ t traj ​ ( c tar ) ] . S_{t}=\frac{1}{2}\left[\Delta_{t}^{\mathrm{traj}}(c_{\mathrm{src}})+\Delta_{t}^{\mathrm{traj}}(c_{\mathrm{tar}})\right]. (6) By construction, the two terms form an exact additive decomposition of the base edit field, A t = P t + S t . A_{t}=P_{t}+S_{t}. (7) Consequently, the decomposition preserves the update prescribed by the base editor while explicitly seperating the prompt-induced and trajectory-induced changes. Experiments Experimental Setup Evaluation Datasets and Metrics. We evaluate CEF on all 700 examples in PIE-Bench ( Ju et al. 2024 ) . We measure alignment with the target prompt using CLIP similarity ( Radford et al. 2021 ) between the prompt and either the complete edited image (CLIP-W) or the annotated edit region (CLIP-E). Source preservation is evaluated using DINO-based Structure Distance ( Ju et al. 2024 ; Caron et al. 2021 ) over the complete image, together with PSNR, MSE, LPIPS ( Zhang et al. 2018 ) , and SSIM ( Wang et al. 2004 ) over the region outside the edit. Benchmark masks define the edited region and the remaining image only for evaluation and are not accessed by CEF. Implementation Details. We implement CEF using Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium ( Esser et al. 2024 ; Stability AI 2024 ) and FLUX ( Black Forest Labs 2024 ) as the backbone models, while keeping all generative models frozen. For direct comparison, we use the sampling configurations of FlowEdit ( Kulikov et al. 2025 ) : ( T , n max ) = ( 50 , 33 ) (T,n_{\max})=(50,33) for SD3.5 and ( T , n max ) = ( 28 , 24 ) (T,n_{\max})=(28,24) for FLUX, with n avg = 1 n_{\mathrm{avg}}=1 for both. Conclusion We propose CEF, a training-free method, to address unintended source changes caused by edit responses accumulating outside the requested region along editing trajectories. CEF estimates continuous edit responsibility from visual evidence, decomposes the base edit field into prompt-induced and trajectory-induced components, and spatially constrains their contributions at each editing step. This design suppresses unrelated changes without uniformly weakening the editing trajectory. Across all 700 PIE-Bench examples, CEF achieves state-of-the-art source preservation with SD3.5 Medium and FLUX while maintaining edit alignment.
